tag: Schools, workplaces & study — always in use
bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: notice that the exact same sentence frames ("I enjoy it because...", "I don't mind + -ing, but...") work whether you're a pupil, a student, or a working professional — learn the frame once, then just plug in whatever's true for you.

questions.text: Are you a student? What school do you go to?
questions.model: Yeah, I am. I'm currently studying Computer Science at Webster University in Tashkent. It's quite challenging at times, but I enjoy it because I've always been interested in technology and how things work.
usefulLanguage: be interested in how something works

questions.text: What's your favourite subject at school?
questions.model: I'd probably say Computer Science. I like subjects where I actually have to think and solve problems rather than just memorise a lot of information. It can be frustrating sometimes, but I find it really satisfying when I finally figure something out.

questions.text: Do you like your school?
questions.model: Yeah, overall, I do. I like the people there, and I think the atmosphere is pretty relaxed, so I feel comfortable studying there. Of course, there are a few things I'd change, but nothing major.
usefulStructure: There are a few things I'd change, but...

questions.text: What do you dislike about school?
questions.model: Probably the amount of work we sometimes get. There are periods when several assignments pile up at once, and then I have to spend most of my free time studying. I don't mind working hard, but I don't really enjoy having no time to switch off.

questions.text: What do you want to do after you finish school?
questions.model: Once I finish my studies, I'd like to get some experience in the tech industry, probably in software development or AI. I'm still figuring out exactly what I want to specialise in, though. For now, I just want to keep learning and see where it takes me.
usefulLanguage: figure out what I want to...
usefulStructure: Once + present simple, I'd like to + verb

questions.text: Are you a student? What are you studying?
questions.model: Yes, I am. I'm studying Computer Science, and most of what I'm doing at the moment is related to programming and problem-solving. It's not always easy, but I like the fact that there's usually a clear solution to work towards.
usefulStructure: Most of what I'm doing at the moment is + noun/-ing

questions.text: Why did you choose to study that subject?
questions.model: I chose it mainly because I've always been curious about technology. I also enjoy solving problems, and I like the idea of creating something from scratch rather than just using something that already exists. So I felt like Computer Science would suit me quite well.

questions.text: What do you like about your course?
questions.model: What I like most is that it's quite practical. We learn the theory, but we also have to use it to solve actual problems, which makes the classes more interesting. I also like the fact that I'm learning something that could be useful in my future career.

questions.text: Is there anything you dislike about your studies?
questions.model: Yeah, probably the workload. Around exam time, I can have several things to prepare for at once, so it gets a bit overwhelming. I sometimes end up putting off other things because I need to focus on my studies.

questions.text: What do you plan to do after you graduate?
questions.model: I'd like to start working in the tech industry, ideally in software development or something related to AI. At first, I'd probably focus on gaining experience and learning from people who are more experienced than me. Then, once I know the field better, I might think about starting my own projects or business.
usefulStructure: Once + present simple, I might + verb

questions.text: Do you work? What do you do?
questions.model: Yeah, I do. I work as an IELTS instructor at a learning centre, so I help students prepare for their exams, mainly by working on their speaking, writing, reading and listening skills. It can be quite demanding, but I really enjoy seeing students improve.

questions.text: Why did you choose that job?
questions.model: I got into teaching because I enjoy working with people, and I like explaining things in a way that's easy to understand. I also find it really rewarding when a student struggles with something at first but eventually gets it. So, yeah, I guess teaching was a pretty natural choice for me.

questions.text: What do you like about your job?
questions.model: Probably the best thing is seeing my students make progress. When someone comes into my class struggling with a particular skill and then improves over time, it's a really good feeling. I also like that every student is different, so I'm not doing exactly the same thing every day.

questions.text: Is there anything you dislike about your job?
questions.model: I'd say the workload can be a bit much sometimes. When I have a lot of students, there's usually quite a lot of preparation and marking to do, so it can take up most of my free time. I don't mind being busy, but I do need some time to relax and switch off.
usefulLanguage: the workload can be a bit much

questions.text: Do you think you'll stay in this job for a long time?
questions.model: I'm not sure, to be honest. I really enjoy teaching, so I can definitely see myself doing it for a few more years, but I'm also interested in technology and AI. I might eventually move into a different field, but I don't feel like I need to make that decision right now.

topStructures.note: These are the ones I'd actually want students to learn and reuse, rather than memorise dozens of expressions:

items.example: It's best known for its historic architecture.

items.pattern: I'd say the biggest difference is...
items.example: I'd say the biggest difference is the pace of life.
I could see myself living in the countryside one day.
I like the idea of living somewhere quieter.

items.pattern: X tends to be..., whereas Y...
items.example: City life tends to be busier, whereas the countryside is much quieter.

items.pattern: There are more... than there used to be
items.example: There are more modern buildings than there used to be.
I've never actually lived in the countryside.
Even though I live elsewhere now, I still feel connected to my hometown.
I go back whenever I get the chance.
I find the countryside relaxing because there's less noise.

topStructures.closingNote: These are much more valuable for an 8+ student than memorising a long list of "advanced" hometown vocabulary. They give the student structures they can actually recycle naturally across dozens of Part 1 topics.

questions.text: Please describe your hometown a little.
questions.model: I'm from Bukhara, which is a fairly old city in Uzbekistan. It's probably best known for its historic buildings and traditional architecture, and there are quite a few places that date back hundreds of years. At the same time, it's a fairly quiet place, so life there is a lot slower-paced than in a big city.
usefulStructure: It's probably best known for + noun

questions.text: What is your hometown well-known for?
questions.model: It's mainly known for its history and architecture. There are lots of old mosques, madrasas and other historic sites, so quite a few tourists visit the city every year. I'd say that's probably the main thing that sets it apart from other cities in the country.
usefulLanguage: sets it apart from = makes it different from
usefulStructure: I'd say that's probably the main thing that...

questions.text: Do you like your hometown?
questions.model: Yeah, I do, especially because I grew up there. I have a lot of good memories of the place, and I still enjoy going back whenever I get the chance. It's not perfect, of course, but there's something familiar and comforting about it.
usefulLanguage: go back whenever I get the chance
usefulStructure: I enjoy + -ing whenever I get the chance.

questions.text: Is that a big city or a small place?
questions.model: I'd say it's somewhere in between. It's not a tiny town, but it's definitely smaller and quieter than places like Tashkent. Most parts of the city are pretty easy to get around, so you don't have to spend ages stuck in traffic.
usefulStructure: It's not X, but it's definitely Y.

questions.text: How long have you been living there?
questions.model: I grew up there, so I lived there for most of my childhood. I moved away later on for university and work, but I still go back from time to time to see my family and friends. So, even though I don't live there anymore, I still feel quite connected to the place.
usefulLanguage: go back from time to time

questions.text: Do you think you will continue living there for a long time?
questions.model: Probably not, to be honest. I like my hometown, but I think I'd prefer to live somewhere with more career opportunities, especially as I'm interested in technology. I could see myself living in a bigger city for a few years, although I'd probably like to go back there eventually.

questions.text: Would you like to live in the countryside in the future?
questions.model: Yeah, possibly, but probably not permanently. I like the idea of living somewhere quiet and surrounded by nature, especially after spending years in a busy city. But I think I'd get bored if I lived too far away from shops, restaurants and other things to do.
usefulStructure: I'd get + adjective if + past simple

questions.text: Have you ever lived in the countryside?
questions.model: No, not really. I've spent quite a lot of time in rural areas when visiting relatives, but I've never actually lived there on a long-term basis. I think it would be an interesting experience, though, just because it's so different from my usual lifestyle.
usefulStructure: I've spent quite a lot of time + -ing

questions.text: Do you ever spend time in the countryside?
questions.model: Yeah, from time to time. I sometimes go out to the countryside with friends or family, especially when I want to get away from the noise and crowds. I find it quite relaxing because you can slow down a bit and just enjoy being outdoors.
usefulLanguage: get away from the noise and crowds
usefulStructure: especially when I want to + verb

questions.text: What is the difference between living in the countryside and the city?
questions.model: I think the biggest difference is the pace of life. City life tends to be much busier, with more traffic, people and things going on, whereas the countryside is generally quieter. The countryside can be more peaceful, but the city is usually more convenient in terms of jobs, entertainment and public transport.
usefulStructure: X tends to be..., whereas Y is...

questions.text: What do people living in the countryside like to do?
questions.model: I suppose it depends on the person, but people probably spend more time outdoors and with their families. Things like gardening, looking after animals or simply spending time in nature are probably quite common. There's generally less of a rush, so people may have more time to socialise with their neighbours.
usefulStructure: Things like X, Y and Z are...

questions.text: What do you like to do in the countryside?
questions.model: I mostly enjoy just taking a break from my usual routine. If I'm with friends, we might go for a walk, have a picnic or just sit around and talk. I don't really need to do anything special; being somewhere quiet is enough for me.
usefulLanguage: take a break from my usual routine
usefulStructure: I don't really need to..., ... is enough for me.

questions.text: How has your town changed over the last 20 years?
questions.model: It's changed quite a lot, actually. There are more modern buildings and businesses than there used to be, and the city has become more developed in general. At the same time, a lot of the historic parts have been preserved, so it still has that old-city feel, which I think is one of its best features.
usefulLanguage: more ... than there used to be
usefulStructure: There are more... than there used to be.

items.example: I like the fact that it gets a lot of natural light.
I'd probably make the kitchen bigger.
I could see myself moving into a house later on.

items.pattern: If I had to pick one thing, it would be...
items.example: If I had to pick one thing, it would be the lack of storage.
The downside is that I have to do everything myself.
I've been living here for a few months.
I'm still getting used to the neighbourhood.
Apart from that, I'm quite happy with the flat.
That said, I could see myself living in a house later on.
So far, I'm quite happy with it.

questions.text: Can you describe the place where you live?
questions.model: Sure. I live in a fairly modern flat in Tashkent. It's not particularly large, but there's enough space for everything I need, and I like the fact that it gets quite a lot of natural light during the day. It's also in a pretty convenient area, so most things I need are within easy reach.
usefulLanguage: quite a lot of natural light
usefulStructure: I like the fact that + clause

questions.text: What kind of housing accommodation do you live in?
questions.model: I live in a rented flat at the moment. It's a fairly typical apartment for the area, with a couple of bedrooms, a living room and a small kitchen. I think a flat suits me better than a house because it's easier to look after.
usefulStructure: I think X suits me better because...

questions.text: What do you like about your flat?
questions.model: Probably the location. It's close to pretty much everything I need, so I don't have to spend a lot of time travelling around the city. I also like the living room because it's quite spacious and a nice place to unwind after a long day.

questions.text: Which room does your family spend most of the time in?
questions.model: Probably the living room. That's where we usually sit down and chat, watch TV or have something to eat together. It's also the most comfortable room in the flat, so it naturally becomes the main gathering place.

questions.text: What can you see from the windows where you live?
questions.model: There's not much of a view, to be honest. I can mainly see the buildings and streets around us, and there are a few trees as well. It's nothing spectacular, but I do like having some greenery outside rather than just looking at concrete buildings.
usefulLanguage: the buildings and streets around us
usefulStructure: There's not much of a + noun.

questions.text: Do you prefer living in a house or a flat?
questions.model: I'd probably choose a flat, at least for now. I like the fact that everything is relatively easy to manage, and I don't have to worry about things like a garden or a large amount of maintenance. That said, I could see myself moving into a house later on, especially if I have a family.

questions.text: What would you like to change in your flat?
questions.model: I'd probably make the kitchen a bit bigger. It's perfectly fine as it is, but there isn't much room to move around, especially when more than one person is using it. I'd also like to add some more storage space because we tend to run out of space pretty quickly.
usefulLanguage: there isn't much room to move around
usefulStructure: It's fine as it is, but...

questions.text: What do you dislike about your flat?
questions.model: If I had to pick one thing, it would probably be the lack of storage. We have enough space overall, but there's nowhere to put some of the bigger things, so the flat can look a little cluttered. Apart from that, I'm quite happy with it.
usefulStructure: If I had to pick one thing, it would be...

questions.text: Who do you live with?
questions.model: At the moment, I live on my own. I actually quite like it because I have a lot more privacy and freedom, and I can organise my day however I want. The downside is that I have to do everything myself, but I'm pretty used to it now.

questions.text: How long have you lived there?
questions.model: I've been living there for a few months now. I moved in fairly recently, so I'm still getting used to the place and the neighbourhood. But so far, I'm quite happy with it, and I think I've settled in pretty well.
